text: Initial direction: test whether P’s dynamic reference-frame and kinematic-link logic can extend from end-effector poses to Q’s tendon-driven grasp, where only seven motor encoders are observed. I am checking the exact observability and contact assumptions before claiming a combination. Q: inputs/Q.tex, Observation and action; P: inputs/P.tex, Technical Approach.

Initial reading: Q gives an encoder-only, seven-motor tendon hand with an identified actuator map and contact-rich cube rotation; P gives dynamic object-frame stream selection for moving objects and bimanual coordination. I am checking whether P’s inferred rigid links and pose-frame policy can remain well-defined when the manipulating hand has only motor encoders, elastic underactuation, and changing contacts, and whether Q’s tendon simulator supplies a controlled test.

Candidate cross-paper gap: P identifies endogenous object frames by near-zero variance of object-relative end-effector pose (inputs/P.tex, Manipulation in Dynamic Environments, Eq. gmsd) and filters linked frames from product-of-experts. Q trains sustained in-hand cube rotation while maintaining a grasp (inputs/Q.tex, Learning In-Hand Cube Rotation; Results). There the cube can be caused by the hand while deliberately moving relative to the palm, so rigid-link/low-variance is not necessary for endogeneity. Research question: can frame selection detect action-caused, nonrigid contact rather than only rigid co-motion? Q supplies a tendon-level simulator and motor-command map with which to test this. Need check P for other detection signals and Q for observable object pose constraints.

A sharper point beyond rigid slip: P computes per-time Gaussian stream covariance and declares a link when its geometric mean deviation is below threshold (inputs/P.tex, Eq. gmsd). This statistic cannot identify physical rigidity. If demonstrations follow a repeatable in-hand rotation (T_{HO}(t)=T_0R_z(\omega t)) with small across-demo noise, the object moves relative to the hand yet has arbitrarily low covariance at each phase, so P will label a link. Conversely action-caused slip with high variation can evade the threshold. This is a statistical identifiability claim, not evidence that P fails empirically on Q. I am checking whether the practical consequence is a lost object-orientation feedback channel and what an implementable intervention test would require.
Correction to #4 notation: \(T_{HO}(t)=T_0R_z(\omega t)\). The mechanism is a repeatable relative rotation with small variance across demonstrations at fixed phase.

Refinement of #3: P’s precision is the stream covariance at a given trajectory/skill phase across demonstrations, not simply temporal variance along one rollout (inputs/P.tex, Multi-Stream Policy Learning and Eq. gmsd). A cube rotating relative to the palm does not by itself prove P will miss a link: perfectly phase-aligned rotation could still give near-zero covariance. The defensible claim is that rigid coupling guarantees a fixed relative pose, whereas contact with slip or finger gaiting does not guarantee low phase-conditioned covariance. A variable-speed/phase in-hand rotation is the specific stress test; its failure remains to be measured.

A stronger exact counterexample to P’s causal reading of stream precision: an external object on a moving belt with the robot precisely tracking it and a grasped object precisely following the robot can have the same observational joint distribution of object and end-effector poses, hence the same Gaussian stream covariance and (M_t^{(f)}), but opposite causal directions. For any nonsingular joint Gaussian with covariance (\Sigma_{EF}), factor it as either (p(F)p(E\mid F)) or (p(E)p(F\mid E)); the former admits (F\to E), the latter (E\to F). Intervening on the robot separates them: (F) responds only in the latter. P calls its conditional density interventional at inputs/P.tex lines 535-543 and uses only Eq. gmsd at 597-612. This is an identifiability issue independent of rigid versus slipping contact. Q supplies seven calibrated motor channels and a tendon simulator for randomized small action probes (inputs/Q.tex, Actuation Mapping; Tendon-Driven Simulation Model), but physical object response requires P-style external pose tracking because Q logs no object pose on hardware (inputs/Q.tex, Zero-shot deployment).

Important implementation limit: P's streams take the measured end-effector pose and tracked object poses, and predict absolute end-effector poses (inputs/P.tex, Multi-Stream Policy Learning). Q's deployed rotation policy sees only seven encoder-derived channels and the previous action, while its \(7\times16\) joint-to-actuation map has rank seven and the physical cube pose is not logged (inputs/Q.tex, joint-to-actuation model; Observation and action; Zero-shot deployment). Thus P cannot simply be attached to Q's existing policy. A real test needs external cube pose tracking and an explicit adapter from object-frame goals to Q's seven cable commands; the simulator can test the causal gate first.

Longer derivation and test plan are in ada/causal_frame_note.md. The exact Gaussian construction shows that observational (M_t^{(f)}) can be identical for (F\to E) and (E\to F), so P’s precision threshold is not a causal-direction identifier, although its reported tasks may still work. A randomized motor-command perturbation and measured object response separates these cases; Q’s seven-channel map and simulator make that test concrete, but real hardware requires external object tracking (Q does not log cube pose). Publication requires measured failure of frame selection plus improvement, not just the counterexample. Relevant prior work: https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.13165 and https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.12160. Search queries and scope are recorded in the note; no novelty claim.

Notation correction to #7 and #9: the stream statistic is \(M_t^{(f)}\), and the two possible directions are \(F\to E\) and \(E\to F\). The Gaussian proof and all mathematics appear with valid TeX delimiters in ada/causal_frame_note.md.

Cross-check of emmy #4: low covariance during a repeatable in-hand rotation is indeed possible, but P masking that frame is not necessarily an error if the hand causes the motion. The consequential tests are (i) sustained exogenous tracking with low covariance, which gives a false positive, and (ii) action-caused cube rotation with variable phase/contact mode and high covariance, which gives a false negative. The exact observational equivalence in ada/causal_frame_note.md makes (i) independent of any conjecture about Q rollout variability. P already notes only brief pre-grasp spikes, not sustained tracking (inputs/P.tex, footnote after Eq. gmsd).

My best account: P's geometric mean stream spread is an observational proxy for a kinematic link, but cannot establish whether the robot drives the frame; ada/causal_frame_note.md proves identical pose statistics can arise from opposite causal directions. Q contributes a calibrated seven-channel intervention interface and contact-rich cube-rotation simulator that can test a direction-sensitive gate. The question is now whether such a gate improves frame selection in sustained exogenous tracking and variable-phase in-hand manipulation. Unresolved: whether these failures occur in P's implementation at meaningful rates, how to map P's pose-stream actions to Q's tendon commands, real cube-pose tracking, and whether the result is distinct from prior contact/causal inference work. I claim a falsifiable publication path, not an established performance gain or novelty.

I wrote the derivation and minimal experiment at emmy/causal-frame-test.md. Core result: if per-phase local pose covariance is \(\Sigma_t=\epsilon^2 I_6\), P's Eq. gmsd gives \(M_t=\epsilon\) whether the relative pose is rigid or follows a repeatable rotation \(T_{HO}(t)=T_0R_z(\omega t)\). The decisive paired-rollout test in Q's simulator changes one motor target at matched initial conditions, measures future cube-pose response, and compares this interventional label against P's precision gate across rigid holding, rotation, slip, and exogenous motion. This is a diagnostic before any claim of improved policy success. Prior-work check queries included "robot manipulation detect contact mode action interventions object motion causal frame policy arxiv" and "in hand manipulation underactuated tendon hand visual feedback object pose sim to real arxiv"; visual reorientation and pose feedback already exist (https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.11744; https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.02843), so the possible angle is causal frame selection, not vision alone.

Cross-check of emmy #13 and emmy/causal-frame-test.md: the calculation \(M_t=\epsilon\) for \(\Sigma_t=\epsilon^2I_6\) is correct, and the note appropriately avoids claiming empirical failure. Its factorization argument is made constructive by the two opposite-direction structural Gaussian models in ada/causal_frame_note.md. I agree the paired-rollout classification test is the first decisive experiment. For a policy-level claim, a second experiment must show that the new gate improves selection or success under the same pose observations; Q's encoder-only deployed controller does not already provide that input or a pose-to-tendon adapter. No disagreement remains on the core claim.

Distinct pair-specific issue after cross-checking ada's note: P's scalar \(M_t^{(f)}=(\det\Sigma_t^{(f)})^{1/12}\) is the geometric mean of six local pose standard deviations. Q's cube task rotates mainly about one axis while the hand retains the cube spatially (inputs/Q.tex, Learning In-Hand Cube Rotation; Results). In a diagonal local covariance with five constrained directions of standard deviation \(\epsilon\) and a free yaw direction of standard deviation \(s\), \(M=(\epsilon^5s)^{1/6}\). For any large \(s\), sufficiently small \(\epsilon\) trips P's rigid-link threshold, so an all-or-nothing frame mask hides the free yaw degree of freedom. This is a mathematical partial-constraint failure of P's determinant gate, separate from causal-direction nonidentifiability. A possible stronger pair result is subspace-aware frame fusion: mask hand-determined pose components but retain object-relative yaw feedback. Need test whether this improves object-orientation control with a motor-command adapter; Q currently has no physical cube pose sensing.

Qualification to #16: the determinant construction proves P's scalar cannot certify full rigid coupling, but it does not prove that masking the cube harms P's original tasks. For a performance test, add a goal that requires observing cube yaw (target orientation or recovery from an external yaw perturbation), hold perception and the cable-command controller fixed, and compare whole-frame masking with a partial-constraint gate. Q's published encoder-only rotation neither measures physical cube yaw nor tests target tracking, so no performance claim follows from Q alone.

Cross-check of #16: the anisotropic determinant counterexample is valid: for \(\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\epsilon^2,\ldots,\epsilon^2,s^2)\), \(M=(\epsilon^5s)^{1/6}\). P explicitly offers a diagonal weight matrix \(W\) (inputs/P.tex:611), but for fixed nonsingular \(W\), \(\det(W\Lambda W)=\det(W)^2\det\Lambda\); this only rescales the scalar gate and does not identify which pose direction is free. However a subspace-aware frame *fusion* improvement is not established for Q: P predicts absolute end-effector poses and disregards gripper actions (inputs/P.tex:412-418), while Q rotates the cube by seven tendon targets with an approximately fixed palm (inputs/Q.tex:644-669). Retaining cube-yaw information in a palm-pose stream cannot command the fingers without a new action model. Treat #16 as a precise diagnostic of the gate, then require a tendon-action policy/adapter and matched control comparison for the stronger claim.

The #16-17 subspace proposal needs a semantic split. In P, an object pose enters as a task-parameter frame for transforming and fusing *end-effector pose targets* (inputs/P.tex:412-480); masking prevents a robot-driven object from being treated as exogenous (inputs/P.tex:535-553). For a cube yaw goal, the same robot-driven yaw may still be indispensable as *feedback state* to a tendon-command controller. Keeping yaw in P-style pose-frame fusion is not equivalent to retaining yaw as feedback, and the causal action-response gate would label yaw endogenous rather than automatically preserve it. A viable experiment should compare (a) P-style frame mask, (b) direction-sensitive whole-frame mask, and (c) a controller that models object-yaw dynamics/feedback separately, using the same tracked cube pose and seven-channel commands. Q supplies the actuation testbed, not an existing pose-frame policy; a matched tendon policy must be built. This is an unresolved modeling question, not a claimed improvement.

Prior-work check on #16: Calinon's task-parameterized movement-learning tutorial already develops covariance eigenspaces and subspace models for robot skills (https://calinon.ch/papers/Calinon-JIST2015.pdf, Sec. 4). So eigenvalue inspection or a generic subspace policy is not a stand-alone novelty claim. The pair-specific candidate is narrower: whether P's binary dynamic frame mask fails in Q's partially constrained in-hand rotation, and whether preserving the free object-pose component improves a matched tendon-action controller. Search query: "robot task parameterized Gaussian mixture model partial constraints dimensions covariance subspace reference frames manipulation". If the matched controller cannot be built or no failure appears, the result is only a diagnostic limitation.

I expanded ada/causal_frame_note.md with the anisotropic gate derivation and frame-versus-feedback distinction. For a constructed six-dimensional covariance with five standard deviations \(\epsilon\) and yaw standard deviation \(s\), \(M=(\epsilon^5s)^{1/6}\). At \(\epsilon=10^{-4}\), \(s=10^{-1}\), P\x27s \(\tau_M=10^{-3}\) masks the whole frame although yaw spread is \(0.1\) rad. P\x27s suggested fixed diagonal \(W\) changes this scalar only by \(|\det W|^{-1/6}\). This proves a limitation of scalar masking, not an observed error or control loss. The note states assumptions and a matched tendon-policy test. Markdown style checks passed with line-length warnings only.

Correction after ada #19: I agree that "retain yaw" must mean retain cube yaw as feedback to a tendon-action controller, not keep it as an exogenous P-style task frame. P's object frame transforms an absolute end-effector pose expert; Q's cube yaw is a manipulated state. The partial-constraint determinant calculation remains valid as a diagnostic, but subspace-aware frame fusion is not yet a justified remedy. The sharper single question is whether an action-response estimate plus component-level constraint analysis can assign object-pose variables to exogenous guidance versus endogenous feedback, and whether this improves a matched seven-motor controller. The first publishable step is measured frame-role errors, then matched control gains; without those this is only a limitation note.

Correction to #21: the literal escape sequence in P\x27s is a formatting typo; I meant P\x27s threshold and P\x27s suggested weighting. I verified emmy #20 against Calinon\x27s primary tutorial, Section 4, https://calinon.ch/papers/Calinon-JIST2015.pdf : task-parameterized Gaussian models already use covariance eigenspaces and subspace methods. The note now cites this. Thus generic eigenvalue inspection has no stand-alone novelty. The surviving question is whether action-conditioned frame-role assignment matters empirically at Q\x27s changing contacts, with P\x27s binary mask as baseline.

Best account before ready: I sharpened the assigned-pair question from direct P-on-Q transfer to causal role and partial-constraint selection for object pose. P's dynamic multi-stream policy treats low-variance object-relative end-effector pose as a kinematic link and masks the whole object frame (inputs/P.tex, Multi-Stream Policy Learning; Manipulation in Dynamic Environments, Eq. gmsd). Q's tendon hand rotates a grasped cube about one axis with seven motor channels and only encoder input to its deployed policy (inputs/Q.tex, Hand Design; Learning In-Hand Cube Rotation; Zero-shot deployment). A covariance with five narrow directions and free yaw has \(M=(\epsilon^5s)^{1/6}\), so P's scalar can signal a full link despite free yaw; observational covariance also cannot tell object-causes-robot from robot-causes-object (ada/causal_frame_note.md). Q's calibrated simulator makes matched motor interventions and contact labels possible. The first decisive result would measure P gate errors against object response to randomized motor perturbations; a stronger publication needs a matched seven-motor controller that uses endogenous cube yaw as feedback, versus P-style exogenous frame guidance. Neither Q nor P supplies that adapter, Q has no logged physical cube pose, and simulation contact fidelity is unproved. Calinon already treats covariance subspaces (https://calinon.ch/papers/Calinon-JIST2015.pdf), and visual in-hand feedback already exists (https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.11744), so the pair supports a falsifiable path, not a novelty or performance claim. Longer derivation: emmy/causal-frame-test.md.

Formatting correction to #21 and #23: the raw sequence backslash-x-2-7 denotes an apostrophe and has no mathematical meaning. Read the affected phrases as the threshold reported by P and the weighting suggested by P. All substantive equations in #21 remain as written.
